meta.title: Who really said "Walking is man's best medicine"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Hippocrates. Wikiquote files it under Disputed; it appears in none of his surviving works, and no one has traced the English wording to a source.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Walking is man's best medicine'?
meta.ogDescription: Hippocrates never wrote it. The closest real passage, Regimen II.lxii, calls walking natural but adds that there is something violent about it.

answer.label: Not Hippocrates — an unsourced slogan
answer.authorDates: Origin untraced · absent from the Hippocratic Corpus
answer.sourceLine: Wikiquote files this line under Disputed, noting that it “does not occur in any of his surviving works.” Classicist Helen King gave the quote a whole section of Hippocrates Now and could not find where the English sentence came from — the nearest real Hippocratic passage says something conspicuously different, and no researcher has yet traced an originator.

source.heading: The closest thing in the real corpus

docMeta.dd: Found in no surviving Hippocratic text

Walking is a ‘natural’ exercise — with “something violent” about it

source.excerpt: Walking is a natural exercise, much more so than the other exercises, but there is something violent about it.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ files the line under Disputed: it “does not occur in any of his surviving works”, the claim that he ‘said’ it “could not be verified”, and the Loeb Regimen II.LXII sentence is offered as the best match, following Helen King at p.109.

In chapter 5 of Hippocrates Now ↗ Helen King asks outright, “Where does this claim about walking originate?” — and never finds an answer, instead documenting the line as a health-scheme and gym slogan and as the title of a 2012 article in Occupational Medicine.

The trail she follows starts on Wikipedia: in the Talk:Hippocrates archive ↗, an editor opened a thread on 8 October 2017 headed “Walking is man’s best medicine”, writing “I can’t find any evidence that Hippocrates actually said this (and the citation is not persuasive). Can anyone help?” Nobody could.

The one scholarly attempt to ground the slogan, a 2016 paper in the American Journal of Sports Science and Medicine ↗, cites Regimen II.lxi–lxii from the 1931 Loeb — but quotes only as far as “much more so than the other exercises”, and misnames the translator.
source.cutTag: Usually quoted only to the comma
source.excerptNote: Quoted from the 1931 Loeb translation as reproduced by Wikiquote ↗ and discussed by Helen King. The half after the comma is what campaigners drop — and it is the half that stops the sentence being a recommendation of walking above all else.
source.rightsNote: No rights status can be asserted for the popular wording, because no work has ever been shown to contain it — an unsourced English sentence has no identifiable first publication. Separately, the genuine passage excerpted above is quoted from W. H. S. Jones’s Loeb translation, first published in 1931 and therefore not in the public domain in the United States; the ancient Greek of Regimen is of course long out of copyright.

author.name: Hippocrates
author.kicker: The name it gets pinned on
author.heading: Hippocrates of Kos
author.metaLine: c. 460 – c. 370 BC · Greek physician, the ‘Father of Medicine’
author.bio: Hippocrates of Kos is the ancient Greek physician traditionally called the ‘Father of Medicine’, and the name attached to the sprawling body of Greek medical writing known as the Hippocratic Corpus. The catch is that scholars have never settled which — if any — of those treatises he actually wrote: the collection spans different subjects, styles and dates, and could not have come from one hand. That vagueness is exactly what makes him such a convenient signature. A blank where the author should be is easy to fill with whatever a modern wellness slogan needs him to have said.

copyAttribution: "Walking is man's best medicine" is not Hippocrates. Wikiquote files the line under Disputed, noting it does not occur in any of his surviving works, and Helen King's "Hippocrates Now" (Bloomsbury Academic, 2020, ch. 5) searched for the source of the English wording and found none. The closest genuine passage — Regimen II.lxii, in W. H. S. Jones's 1931 Loeb translation — says walking is "a natural exercise, much more so than the other exercises, but there is something violent about it," which is a rather different claim. — Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: What’s wrong with the attribution
misattribution.intro: This is not a case of a slightly garbled real sentence. There is no Hippocratic text behind the wording at all — only a different passage that has been trimmed until it agrees.

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ places it in the Disputed section and records that the aphorism “appears in dozens of journals, books and blogs as a quote attributed to Hippocrates, but does not occur in any of his surviving works” — adding that the common claim that he ‘said’ rather than wrote it “could not be verified” either.

The passage usually offered as proof reads, in the Loeb, “Walking is a natural exercise, much more so than the other exercises” — but Helen King ↗ points out that the sentence does not end there: it continues “… but there is something violent about it”, and that the ‘natural’ exercises the text actually praises are sight, hearing, voice and thought.

King shows how the line is carried by campaigns, gyms and journals rather than by texts — Psychology Today ↗ (Christopher Bergland, 12 June 2015) is typical, calling ‘walking is the best medicine’ Hippocrates’ “sage-like advice” without citing a single work.
Even the one careful citation garbles its source: the 2016 paper ↗ that quotes Regimen II correctly credits the 1931 Loeb translation to ‘E. J. James’, when the translator was W. H. S. Jones ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer is that nobody knows who wrote the sentence. The specialists who looked — Wikiquote ↗ and Helen King ↗ — agree only that Hippocrates did not.

context.heading: How a non-quote became a health-campaign slogan
lead: The line travels because it is useful. Helen King documents it doing duty as a slogan for cardiovascular-health schemes and as marketing copy for gyms, and as the exclamation-marked title of a 2012 article in the journal Occupational Medicine — and it circulates as a meme, usually laid over oceans, mountains or a couple on a beach. Attaching Hippocrates’ name converts a piece of ordinary advice into something with 2,400 years of authority behind it, at no cost, because nobody checks.

The irony is that the Hippocratic writings really do take exercise seriously — they just do not say this. King points to passages where patients are told to take walks with their meals, or to build from twenty stades a day up to a hundred, alongside a blunt caveat: “If walks are beneficial to the patient, let him take them; if they are not, he must keep his body as quiet as possible.” That is a conditional prescription, not a universal superlative. The slogan keeps the ancient endorsement and quietly drops the qualification.
context.detailsSummary: Why the closest match still isn’t the quote
detailsBody: The passage everyone reaches for is Regimen II.lxii, quoted in the 1931 Loeb translation as “Walking is a natural exercise, much more so than the other exercises.” Stop there and it sounds like the slogan. It does not stop there: the sentence continues “… but there is something violent about it.”

King notes that the statement has to be read against the preceding chapter, which sorts exercises into ‘natural’ (kata physin) and ‘violent’ (dia biēs) — and that the natural exercises listed there are not walking at all, but sight, hearing, voice and thought, all of which ‘move the soul’. Her conclusion is that this is “clearly not the world of sports medicine” that the modern slogan belongs to.

There is a further complication about who Hippocrates even is here. King records that Galen already doubted that the first book of Regimen was Hippocratic, allowing only that the second book “might perhaps with good reason be thought worthy of Hippocrates” — and modern scholarship attributes none of the corpus to him with confidence.
context.pull: The corpus recommends walking. It never calls it the best medicine.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists "Walking is man's best medicine" in its Disputed section, stating it "does not occur in any of his surviving works", that the claim he "said" rather than wrote it "could not be verified", and quoting the Loeb Regimen II.LXII sentence "Walking is a natural exercise, much more so than the other exercises, but there is something violent about it", citing Helen King, Hippocrates Now, p.109.

Helen King's chapter 'Hippocrates in Quotes' contains a section headed 'Walking is the best medicine' which asks 'Where does this claim about walking originate?', documents the quote's use as a slogan by health schemes and gyms and as the title of a 2012 article in Occupational Medicine, notes that Nomikos et al. used the 1931 Loeb translation by W.H.S. Jones while misattributing it to 'E.J. James', and shows the Regimen sentence continues '...but there is something violent about it' while the 'natural' exercises listed are sight, hearing, voice and thought.

Bryn Mawr Classical Review confirms Helen King, Hippocrates Now: The 'Father of Medicine' in the Internet Age, Bloomsbury Studies in Classical Reception, London/New York: Bloomsbury Academic, 2020, and that chapter 5 examines 'Walking is the best medicine' as having only a tenuous connection to ancient material.

Nomikos et al., 'The Role of Exercise in Hippocratic Medicine', quotes 'Walking is a natural exercise, much more so than the other exercises' citing Hippocrates, Regimen II.lxi–lxii, Loeb Classical Library, 1931, and credits the translation to 'E. J. James'.

The Wikipedia Talk:Hippocrates archive contains a thread headed "Walking is man's best medicine" posted by user Brownturkey at 16:09, 8 October 2017 (UTC): 'I can't find any evidence that Hippocrates actually said this (and the citation is not persuasive). Can anyone help?'

Wellcome Collection's catalogue record confirms Hippocrates Vol. IV, English translation by W. H. S. Jones, Loeb Classical Library, published 1931 (William Heinemann, London; G. P. Putnam's Sons, New York), containing Regimen I, Regimen II and Regimen III in parallel Greek and English.
Psychology Today (Christopher Bergland, 12 June 2015) attributes 'walking is the best medicine' to Hippocrates as his 'sage-like advice', citing no primary source.

Wikipedia states Hippocrates lived c. 460 – c. 370 BC, was an ancient Greek physician traditionally called the 'Father of Medicine', and that whether he authored any treatise in the Hippocratic Corpus 'has not been conclusively answered' since the collection 'could not have been written by one person'.

NCBI PubMed record 22764266 is Batman DC, "Hippocrates: 'Walking is man's best medicine!'", Occupational Medicine (Oxford, England) 2012 Jul;62(5):320-2, doi 10.1093/occmed/kqs084 — confirming the 2012 Occupational Medicine article King refers to.
